html:
Orbital
The figure opens with all three side by side, as printed; pick one to enlarge it.
Sign highlight
Pink = positive ψ, blue = negative ψ. Click any lobe in the figure to light every lobe of the same sign; the nodal plane(s) fade in.
Nucleus
Guided tour
Drag to orbit · scroll to zoom. Orbiting shows that the p lobes are rotationally symmetric about their axis while the d cloverleaf lies flat in one plane. Press “Reset View” (top) to return to the printed front view.

plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 1: Structure and Bonding
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three rendered orbital shapes in a row on a white background, each captioned in bold beneath it, reading from left to right "An s orbital", "A p orbital", and "A d orbital". The leftmost is one translucent pink sphere, smooth and unbroken in every direction, with a small yellow-green bead at its center marking the nucleus. The middle shape stacks two lobes vertically, a rounded pink one above and a matching blue one below, meeting at a green nucleus bead; both are drawn as full, doorknob-like volumes rather than pointed teardrops, and they pinch away to nothing where they meet. The rightmost carries four lobes in a cloverleaf around a central green bead, their colors alternating around the ring: pink at the upper left and lower right, blue at the upper right and lower left. Color does the encoding, pink and blue standing for opposite algebraic signs of the wave function across a node, so the alternation shows the sign flipping with each crossing from one lobe to the next. The three together set out the orbital shapes and sign patterns that later account for bonding.

elements: s orbital: single translucent pink sphere, smooth and unbroken in all directions
s orbital nucleus: small opaque yellow-green bead at the sphere's exact center
p orbital: two rounded 'doorknob' lobes stacked vertically along the Y axis, pink lobe above, blue lobe below, each pinching to a point where they meet at the origin
p orbital nucleus: small green bead at the pinch point between the two lobes
p orbital nodal plane (horizontal XZ plane through the nucleus, implied by the pinch)

d orbital: four rounded lobes arranged as a cloverleaf in the vertical plane, pointing along the four diagonals; pink at upper-left and lower-right, blue at upper-right and lower-left; all four pinch to the origin
d orbital nucleus: small green bead at the center of the cloverleaf
d orbital's two perpendicular nodal planes crossing at the nucleus
bold caption text beneath each shape: 'An s orbital', 'A p orbital', 'A d orbital'
plain white background, no axes or box

interactions.teaches: s, p and d orbitals differ in lobe count and node structure: zero nodes and one sphere, one node and two lobes, two nodes and four lobes
interactions.label: Orbital

interactions.teaches: pink and blue are not decoration but opposite algebraic signs of the wave function; clicking one lobe lights every lobe of the same sign and shows the sign flipping across each node
each orbital is a genuine 3D volume — the p lobes are rotationally symmetric about their axis and the d cloverleaf lies in a single plane, facts invisible from the printed front view

demo_steps.title: The s orbital
demo_steps.narration: A single pink sphere surrounds the yellow-green nucleus. The wave function has one sign everywhere and no nodes, so there is only one color.

demo_steps.title: The p orbital and its node
demo_steps.narration: Two doorknob lobes meet at the nucleus. The pink lobe above and blue lobe below carry opposite signs; the pinch between them is a nodal plane where the wave function is zero.

demo_steps.title: The d orbital: signs alternate
demo_steps.narration: Four lobes form a cloverleaf, pink at upper-left and lower-right, blue at upper-right and lower-left. Click any lobe to highlight its partner and see the sign flip on every crossing of a node.

demo_steps.title: Compare all three
demo_steps.narration: Side by side, the progression is clear: 0 nodes and 1 lobe, 1 node and 2 lobes, 2 nodes and 4 lobes.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: s sphere radius 1.15 units, centered at origin, nucleus bead radius 0.09. p orbital: two lobes along +Y and -Y, each about 1.25 units long and 0.95 units wide at its fattest, fat end outward, tapering to a cusp at the origin (build as a revolved profile r(theta) = 1.25*|cos(theta)| about the Y axis, or two squashed spheres scaled 0.48 x 0.65 x 0.48 and offset to y = +/-0.72 with the inner ends pinched); pink lobe is the +Y one, blue lobe the -Y one; overall p height ~2.5 units, so it reads slightly taller than the s sphere is wide. d orbital: four identical lobes in the XY plane pointing along the diagonals at +135 deg (pink), +45 deg (blue), -135 deg (blue), -45 deg (pink) measured from +X, each lobe 1.15 units long, 0.85 wide, tapering to the origin; overall d width ~2.4 units, height ~2.4. Nucleus beads sit exactly at the origin of each shape and must render on top of the translucent lobes. When 'all three' is selected, place s at x = -3.4, p at x = 0, d at x = +3.4 with each shape's own origin on the y = 0 line; the single-orbital views center the selected shape at the origin. Bold captions on a plane at y = -2.1 directly under each shape, dark gray #1a1a1a. Colors: pink/rose lobes #dc9aa8 with a lighter #eebcc6 highlight, blue lobes #7fa6d4 with #a8c4e6 highlight, both translucent (opacity ~0.82) with soft matte shading and no hard specular; s-orbital nucleus yellow-green #bcc74a, p and d nuclei green #49a04f. Background pure white, no grid, no axis lines. Sign meaning: pink = positive wave-function amplitude, blue = negative; lobes sharing a color share a sign.
interactionPlan.notes: Use MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission/opacity ~0.8, roughness ~0.7, flatShading off, and DoubleSide so the translucent lobe interiors read like the airbrushed source renders; disable depthWrite on the lobes and sort them back-to-front so overlapping lobes blend softly instead of showing hard intersection seams. Nucleus beads use an opaque standard material with depthWrite on. Lobes can be built once as a single tapered-lobe BufferGeometry (revolved cos-profile) and instanced/rotated for the p and d cases; the s sphere is a high-segment SphereGeometry. Click picking: raycast against lobe meshes, then boost emissive and opacity on every lobe whose sign matches the picked one and dim the opposite-sign lobes to ~0.3 opacity; also fade in a translucent gray nodal plane (or two crossed planes for d) while a highlight is active. Toggle between orbital types with a short cross-fade / scale tween rather than an instant swap, and tween the selected shape to the center for the 'all three' -> single transitions. Lighting: one soft directional light from upper-front-left plus strong hemisphere ambient to match the flat, diffuse illumination of the original. Captions as camera-facing sprites or HTML overlays so they stay legible while orbiting.

authoredContext:
What do orbitals look like? There are four different kinds of orbitals, denoted s, p, d, and f, each with a different shape. Of the four, we’ll be concerned primarily with s and p orbitals because these are the most common in organic and biological chemistry. An s orbital has a spherical shape, with the nucleus at its center; a p orbital has a dumbbell shape with two parts, or lobes; and four of the five d orbitals have a cloverleaf shape with four lobes, as shown in the figure. The fifth d orbital is shaped like an elongated dumbbell with a doughnut around its middle.

The three different p orbitals within a given shell are oriented in space along mutually perpendicular directions, denoted px, py, and pz. As shown in the figure, the two lobes of each p orbital are separated by a region of zero electron density called a node. Furthermore, the two orbital regions separated by the node have different algebraic signs, + and −, in the wave function, as represented by the different colors in the figure and the figure. As we’ll see in Section 1.11, these algebraic signs for different orbital lobes have important consequences with respect to chemical bonding and chemical reactivity.

Representations of s, p, and d orbitals. An s orbital is spherical, a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, and four of the five d orbitals are cloverleaf-shaped. Different lobes of p orbitals are often drawn for convenience as teardrops, but their actual shape is more like that of a doorknob, as indicated.

A characteristic s, p, and d orbital with the nucleus at the center of each. Two cloverleaf-shaped lobes and four cloverleaf-shaped lobes form the p and d orbitals, respectively.

The orbitals in an atom are organized into different layers around the nucleus called electron shells, which are centered around the nucleus and have successively larger size and energy. Different shells contain different numbers and kinds of orbitals, and each orbital within a shell can be occupied by two electrons. The first shell contains only a single s orbital, denoted 1s, and thus holds only 2 electrons. The second shell contains one 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals and thus holds a total of 8 electrons. The third shell contains a 3s orbital, three 3p orbitals, and five 3d orbitals, for a total capacity of 18 electrons. These orbital groupings and their energy levels are shown in the figure.

discrepancies: Default state shows only the s orbital, whereas the source figure is a single three-panel composite (s, p, d side by side); the 'all three' mode exists but is not the opening view, so the at-a-glance match to the source is weaker.

The yellow-green nucleus inside the s sphere is barely visible (rendered dark/gray through the depthWrite:false translucent shell), whereas in the source it is a distinct bright yellow-green bead at the centre.
The s sphere reads as a nearly flat pink disc in the screenshot — very little specular/gradient shading compared with the source's soft volumetric highlight, weakening the 3D read.
Extra annotations not in the source (nodal-plane labels, sign-highlight tinting) appear on interaction; pedagogically useful but not part of the original figure.
evaluation.notes: Correct orbital shapes, sign colours and captions with a rich set of meaningful interactions (orbital switcher, sign highlight with nodal planes, guided tour); main weaknesses are the s-only default view versus the source's three-panel layout and a nearly invisible nucleus/flat-looking sphere shading.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are implementation details (default view should be the three-panel mode, nucleus visibility, and sphere shading) that the generator can fix.

Orbital
The figure opens with all three side by side; pick one to enlarge it.

Pink = positive ψ, blue = negative ψ. Click any lobe in the figure to light every lobe of the same sign; the nodal plane(s) fade in.

Guided tour
Drag to orbit · scroll to zoom. Orbiting shows that the p lobes are rotationally symmetric about their axis while the d cloverleaf lies flat in one plane.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Composition broken: the source shows three clearly separated orbitals in a horizontal row, but the generated figure places them at x = -3.4 / 0 / 3.4 and views them from azimuth 15°/elevation 12°, so the s sphere, p lobes and d cloverleaf visibly overlap and interpenetrate in a diagonal clump instead of reading as three distinct panels.

Lobe profile is wrong: the lathe profile t^1.3·(1-t)^0.5 tapers to a point at the outer end, giving cone/teardrop lobes with pointed tips, whereas the source lobes are blunt, fat 'doorknob' volumes rounded at the far end.

Caption sizing/placement: 'An s orbital' and 'A p orbital' render tiny and sit on top of the geometry rather than as a consistent bold caption row below each orbital as in the source; only 'A d orbital' has the expected weight and position.
Overall scene is small and left-offset in the canvas with a large empty area, so the row-of-three layout of the source is lost at a glance.
Perspective projection with tilt introduces foreshortening/overlap the source (flat, front-on, evenly spaced) does not have; the d cloverleaf in particular is seen obliquely rather than face-on.
evaluation.notes: The three orbital types, colour coding (pink +ψ, blue −ψ) and green/yellow nucleus beads are conceptually right and the control set (orbital selector, sign highlight with nodal planes, nucleus toggle, guided tour) is rich and meaningful, but the default view overlaps the three orbitals into a diagonal clump with pointed cone-like lobes and small, misplaced captions, so it does not read as the clean side-by-side source figure.
action_items: Increase the horizontal spacing (e.g. ±4.5–5.0) and use a near front-on view (azimuth ~0–5°, elevation ~0–5°) so the s, p and d orbitals are visually separated exactly as in the source row.
Change the lathe profile so lobes are blunt/rounded at the outer end (e.g. an ellipsoid pinched to a cusp at the origin) instead of tapering to a sharp point.

plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three rendered orbital shapes in a row on a white background, each captioned in bold beneath it, reading from left to right "An s orbital", "A p orbital", and "A d orbital". The leftmost is one translucent pink sphere, smooth and unbroken in every direction, with a small yellow-green bead at its center marking the nucleus. The middle shape stacks two lobes vertically, a rounded pink one above and a matching blue one below, meeting at a green nucleus bead; both are drawn as full, doorknob-like volumes rather than pointed teardrops, and they pinch away to nothing where they meet. The rightmost carries four lobes in a cloverleaf around a central green bead, their colors alternating around the ring: pink at the upper left and lower right, blue at the upper right and lower left. Color does the encoding, pink and blue standing for opposite algebraic signs of the wave function across a node, so the alternation shows the sign flipping with each crossing from one lobe to the next. The three together set out the orbital shapes and sign patterns that later account for bonding.

p orbital nucleus: small green bead at the pinch point between the two lobes
p orbital nodal plane (horizontal XZ plane through the nucleus, implied by the pinch)

d orbital: four rounded lobes arranged as a cloverleaf in the vertical plane, pointing along the four diagonals; pink at upper-left and lower-right, blue at upper-right and lower-left; all four pinch to the origin
d orbital nucleus: small green bead at the center of the cloverleaf
d orbital's two perpendicular nodal planes crossing at the nucleus

demo_steps.title: The s orbital
demo_steps.narration: A single pink sphere surrounds the yellow-green nucleus. The wave function has one sign everywhere and no nodes, so there is only one color.

demo_steps.title: The p orbital and its node
demo_steps.narration: Two doorknob lobes meet at the nucleus. The pink lobe above and blue lobe below carry opposite signs; the pinch between them is a nodal plane where the wave function is zero.

demo_steps.title: The d orbital: signs alternate
demo_steps.narration: Four lobes form a cloverleaf, pink at upper-left and lower-right, blue at upper-right and lower-left. Click any lobe to highlight its partner and see the sign flip on every crossing of a node.

demo_steps.title: Compare all three
demo_steps.narration: Side by side, the progression is clear: 0 nodes and 1 lobe, 1 node and 2 lobes, 2 nodes and 4 lobes.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: s sphere radius 1.15 units, centered at origin, nucleus bead radius 0.09. p orbital: two lobes along +Y and -Y, each about 1.25 units long and 0.95 units wide at its fattest, fat end outward, tapering to a cusp at the origin (build as a revolved profile r(theta) = 1.25*|cos(theta)| about the Y axis, or two squashed spheres scaled 0.48 x 0.65 x 0.48 and offset to y = +/-0.72 with the inner ends pinched); pink lobe is the +Y one, blue lobe the -Y one; overall p height ~2.5 units, so it reads slightly taller than the s sphere is wide. d orbital: four identical lobes in the XY plane pointing along the diagonals at +135 deg (pink), +45 deg (blue), -135 deg (blue), -45 deg (pink) measured from +X, each lobe 1.15 units long, 0.85 wide, tapering to the origin; overall d width ~2.4 units, height ~2.4. Nucleus beads sit exactly at the origin of each shape and must render on top of the translucent lobes. When 'all three' is selected, place s at x = -3.4, p at x = 0, d at x = +3.4 with each shape's own origin on the y = 0 line; the single-orbital views center the selected shape at the origin. Bold captions on a plane at y = -2.1 directly under each shape, dark gray #1a1a1a. Colors: pink/rose lobes #dc9aa8 with a lighter #eebcc6 highlight, blue lobes #7fa6d4 with #a8c4e6 highlight, both translucent (opacity ~0.82) with soft matte shading and no hard specular; s-orbital nucleus yellow-green #bcc74a, p and d nuclei green #49a04f. Background pure white, no grid, no axis lines. Sign meaning: pink = positive wave-function amplitude, blue = negative; lobes sharing a color share a sign.
interactionPlan.notes: Use MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission/opacity ~0.8, roughness ~0.7, flatShading off, and DoubleSide so the translucent lobe interiors read like the airbrushed source renders; disable depthWrite on the lobes and sort them back-to-front so overlapping lobes blend softly instead of showing hard intersection seams. Nucleus beads use an opaque standard material with depthWrite on. Lobes can be built once as a single tapered-lobe BufferGeometry (revolved cos-profile) and instanced/rotated for the p and d cases; the s sphere is a high-segment SphereGeometry. Click picking: raycast against lobe meshes, then boost emissive and opacity on every lobe whose sign matches the picked one and dim the opposite-sign lobes to ~0.3 opacity; also fade in a translucent gray nodal plane (or two crossed planes for d) while a highlight is active. Toggle between orbital types with a short cross-fade / scale tween rather than an instant swap, and tween the selected shape to the center for the 'all three' -> single transitions. Lighting: one soft directional light from upper-front-left plus strong hemisphere ambient to match the flat, diffuse illumination of the original. Captions as camera-facing sprites or HTML overlays so they stay legible while orbiting.

discrepancies: Lobe shape is wrong: the p and d lobes render as sharp-pointed cones/teardrops with an almost straight taper, whereas the source shows fat, blunt, nearly ellipsoidal lobes that meet at a narrow pinch. This noticeably changes the recognizable orbital silhouette.

Scale relationship is off: in the source all three orbitals are roughly comparable in overall size and the p/d lobes are large and rounded; here the s sphere is much larger and visually dominant while the p and d lobes are slim and small.

Source p orbital is oriented with two fat lobes almost touching side-to-side (wide, squat lobes); generated p lobes are narrow and vertically elongated, losing the characteristic 'dumbbell of two flattened balls' look.
The source d orbital's four lobes visibly overlap/blend near the centre with soft translucent shading; the generated cloverleaf lobes are thin, separated spikes with a clean gap.

Nucleus bead colour in the source s orbital is a pale olive/yellow dot and in p/d a green dot — reproduced — but the generated beads are larger and more saturated/emissive than the subtle beads in the source.
Extra annotation labels ('nodal plane (ψ = 0)', 'two nodal planes') and translucent nodal plane geometry are added that do not exist in the source figure (though they only appear during highlight).
evaluation.notes: Composition, colours, captions and interactions closely follow the source and the pedagogy (signs, nodes, nucleus) is sound, but the lobe profile came out as sharp cones rather than the fat blunt lobes of the printed figure, and the s sphere is disproportionately large relative to the p/d orbitals.

feedback.rationale: The concept, composition, and interactions are correct; the issues are implementation details — lobe geometry profile (blunt ellipsoidal instead of sharp cones), relative scaling of s vs p/d, and overly saturated nucleus beads — which are generator-level fixes.
